title: So and such: degree, noun phrases and results
summary: Intensify adjectives and adverbs with so, intensify noun phrases with such (and such a/an), connect an unusually strong degree to its result using so/such ... that, and distinguish so much/many from such a lot of and no such.
learningObjectives: Choose so before adjectives and adverbs and such before singular or plural noun phrases.
Use such a or such an with a singular countable noun and such with plural or uncountable nouns.
Explain consequences naturally using so ... that and such ... that, including cases where that is omitted.
Use so much, so many, so long, so far and such a lot of with the appropriate noun or expression.
Recognise so and such meaning “to that degree / of that kind”, including the negative expression no such.

explanation.heading: So strengthens adjectives and adverbs
explanation.body: Put so directly before an adjective or adverb when the quality or manner is unusually strong: so helpful, so noisy, so carefully. So does not take the place of an article before a normal singular countable noun. When a noun follows, check whether the phrase needs such instead.
explanation.example: The final question was so difficult that we needed extra time.

explanation.heading: Such introduces a whole noun phrase
explanation.body: Use such before a noun phrase: such interesting ideas, such generous support. With a singular countable noun, put a/an after such and before the adjective: such a thoughtful reply or such an unusual request. Use such directly with plurals or uncountable nouns; do not add a/an in those cases.
explanation.example: It was such an inspiring talk that several students joined the project.

explanation.heading: So or such can introduce a result
explanation.body: Use so + adjective/adverb + that and such + (a/an) + noun phrase + that to show why something happened. The second clause gives a consequence, not just another description. In everyday English, speakers often omit that without changing the underlying cause-and-result meaning.
explanation.example: The service was so slow that several customers left before ordering.

explanation.heading: Quantity patterns: so much, so many and such a lot of
explanation.body: Use so much with an uncountable noun and so many with a plural countable noun: so much noise, so many messages. Such a lot of works before both countable plurals and uncountable nouns: such a lot of messages, such a lot of noise. Do not say such many or so a lot of.
explanation.example: We received so many applications that we scheduled another interview day.

explanation.heading: So and such can point to degree or kind
explanation.body: So can mean to that degree, as in I did not expect the hall to be so large; such can mean of that kind, as in I had never heard such a suggestion. The expression no such + noun indicates that the described thing does not exist or is not available in the relevant setting.
explanation.example: There is no such option on the registration form.

explanation.heading: Common fixed patterns with long and far
explanation.body: So long and so far express degree of time and distance without a following noun: we waited so long; it is so far. When a countable noun is included, use such a long time and such a long way. The presence of a noun changes the grammatical pattern.
explanation.example: We travelled such a long way that everyone was ready for a rest.

comparisons.title: Adjective without a noun versus adjective with a noun

left.label: So + adjective
left.note: Noisy is an adjective without a following noun in this structure.

right.label: Such + adjective + noun
right.example: It was such a noisy room.
right.note: Room is singular and countable, so such needs a before the adjective and noun.

comparisons.title: Singular countable versus plural or uncountable nouns

left.label: Singular countable noun
left.example: It was such an unusual idea.
left.note: Such an precedes an adjective plus a singular countable noun.

right.label: Plural noun
right.note: Such can precede a plural noun phrase without a/an.

comparisons.title: Degree of quantity versus a noun phrase

left.label: So much / so many
left.example: We had so much work to finish.
left.note: Much modifies the uncountable noun work.

right.label: Such a lot of
right.example: We had such a lot of work to finish.
right.note: A lot of forms part of the noun phrase introduced by such.

examples.sentence: The new system was so intuitive that nobody needed a manual.
examples.note: So intensifies the adjective intuitive and that introduces the result.

examples.sentence: We had such a productive meeting that we finished the plan early.
examples.note: Such a introduces a singular countable noun phrase.

examples.sentence: It was such terrible weather that the outdoor event was postponed.
examples.note: Weather is uncountable, so such is used without a/an.

examples.sentence: So many people joined the video call that the organiser muted everyone.
examples.note: So many modifies a plural countable noun.

examples.sentence: I did not know the village was so far from the main road.
examples.note: So far expresses an unexpectedly large distance without a noun.

examples.sentence: There is no such rule in the staff handbook.
examples.note: No such means a rule of that description does not exist there.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The instructions were such complicated that I called for help.
commonMistakes.correct: The instructions were so complicated that I called for help.
commonMistakes.why: Use so directly before an adjective when no noun follows.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We saw so a beautiful view from the balcony.
commonMistakes.correct: We saw such a beautiful view from the balcony.
commonMistakes.why: Such a introduces an adjective plus a singular countable noun.

commonMistakes.incorrect: There were such many visitors that the car park filled up.
commonMistakes.correct: There were so many visitors that the car park filled up.
commonMistakes.why: So many is the quantity expression before plural countable nouns.

commonMistakes.incorrect: That was a such surprising result.
commonMistakes.correct: That was such a surprising result.
commonMistakes.why: The article a follows such, not precedes it.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We have waited for so long time.
commonMistakes.correct: We have waited for such a long time.
commonMistakes.why: Use such a long time when the noun time is included in this fixed expression.

studyTips: Circle the head noun in each phrase: if it is present, practise such (a/an) + noun phrase; if only an adjective or adverb follows, practise so.
Build cause-and-result pairs aloud: The task was so difficult that ... / It was such a difficult task that ... .
Keep a short list of useful chunks: so much traffic, so many visitors, such a lot of work, so far and no such rule.

exercises.prompt: The documentary was ___ interesting that I watched it twice.
exercises.feedback: So comes before the adjective interesting; the following clause gives a result.

exercises.prompt: It was ___ unusual proposal that the committee asked for more details.
exercises.feedback: Proposal is a singular countable noun, and unusual begins with a vowel sound: such an unusual proposal.

exercises.prompt: The team has made ___ progress this week that we can finish early.
exercises.feedback: Progress is uncountable, so the quantity pattern is so much progress.

exercises.prompt: There is ___ thing as a perfect schedule; something always changes.
exercises.feedback: No such thing means a thing of this kind does not exist.

exercises.prompt: The presenter spoke ___ clearly that nobody asked for a repetition. (one intensifier)
acceptedAnswers: so
exercises.feedback: So modifies the adverb clearly and connects the degree to the result.

exercises.prompt: We had ___ lovely weather that we spent the afternoon outside. (one intensifier before an uncountable noun)
acceptedAnswers: such
exercises.feedback: Weather is uncountable, so use such lovely weather without an article.

exercises.prompt: He is ___ reliable colleague that everyone asks him for advice. (two words, including the article)
acceptedAnswers: such a
exercises.feedback: Such a comes before an adjective and singular countable noun: such a reliable colleague.

exercises.prompt: ___ people applied for the position that the interviews took a week. (two words meaning a large number)
acceptedAnswers: so many
exercises.feedback: So many introduces an unusually large number of people.

exercises.prompt: Correct the intensifier: The instructions were such confusing that we called support.
acceptedAnswers: The instructions were so confusing that we called support.
exercises.feedback: So modifies the adjective confusing; there is no noun after it.

exercises.prompt: Correct the intensifier and article: We had so a long meeting that everyone missed lunch.
acceptedAnswers: We had such a long meeting that everyone missed lunch.
exercises.feedback: Such a introduces the adjective plus singular countable noun meeting.

exercises.prompt: Correct the intensifier: She was such tired that she slept through the alarm.
acceptedAnswers: She was so tired that she slept through the alarm.
exercises.feedback: So, not such, comes directly before the adjective tired.

exercises.prompt: Correct the quantity expression: There were such many messages that the inbox froze.
acceptedAnswers: There were so many messages that the inbox froze.
exercises.feedback: So many is the correct expression before the plural countable noun messages.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use “so ... that” to combine these facts in one sentence: the laptop / be heavy; I / need both hands to carry it. Begin “The laptop”.
acceptedAnswers: The laptop was so heavy that I needed both hands to carry it.
The laptop was so heavy I needed both hands to carry it.
speakingExercises.feedback: So modifies heavy, and the last clause expresses the consequence.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe the restaurant as unusually noisy and say you ate outside as a result. Begin “It was”, use “such a noisy restaurant that”, and finish “we ate outside”.
acceptedAnswers: It was such a noisy restaurant that we ate outside.
It was such a noisy restaurant we ate outside.
speakingExercises.feedback: Such a introduces the singular noun phrase a noisy restaurant.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence beginning “They asked” using: so many questions / the meeting ran late. Join the clauses with that.
acceptedAnswers: They asked so many questions that the meeting ran late.
speakingExercises.feedback: So many expresses an unusually large number of questions, leading to the result.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend asks why you left the beach early. It was extremely crowded. Reply in one sentence beginning “The beach” and using “so crowded that we left early”.
acceptedAnswers: The beach was so crowded that we left early.
speakingExercises.feedback: So crowded describes degree; the result explains why you left.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say that the announcement was extremely good news and everyone celebrated as a result. Begin “It was” and use “such good news that”.
acceptedAnswers: It was such good news that everyone celebrated.
speakingExercises.feedback: News is uncountable, so use such good news without a/an.

speakingExercises.prompt: The manager says a particular rule does not exist. Say one complete sentence beginning “There is” and ending “such rule”. Include no.
acceptedAnswers: There is no such rule.
There's no such rule.
speakingExercises.feedback: No such rule denies the existence of a rule of that kind.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce exactly two sentences in order. First: the queue / be / so long. Second: it / be / such a busy morning. Use past simple.
acceptedAnswers: The queue was so long. It was such a busy morning.
speakingExercises.feedback: So comes before long alone; such a comes before the noun phrase busy morning.

speakingExercises.prompt: You expected the station to be nearby, but it is far away. Begin “I did not know” and end “so far away”. Say one complete sentence.
acceptedAnswers: I did not know the station was so far away.
I didn't know the station was so far away.
speakingExercises.feedback: So far expresses a surprisingly large distance without adding a noun.

listeningExercises.audioText: The room was so quiet that we could hear the clock ticking from across the hall.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did the unusual quiet allow people to hear?
listeningExercises.feedback: So quiet that introduces the consequence: even the clock could be heard.

listeningExercises.audioText: There were so many people at the entrance that we waited twenty minutes to get inside.
choices: There was a large crowd at the entrance.
listeningExercises.feedback: So many people identifies the unusually large crowd responsible for the wait.

listeningExercises.audioText: That was such a good idea that we used it in the final plan.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two words immediately after “was”.
acceptedAnswers: such a
listeningExercises.feedback: Such a comes before the singular countable noun phrase good idea.

listeningExercises.audioText: There was such heavy rain that the organisers cancelled the outdoor concert.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the result of the weather?
choices: The event continued despite the rain.
listeningExercises.feedback: Such heavy rain introduces the reason, and the audio states that the outdoor concert was cancelled.

listeningExercises.audioText: The new café is so popular that customers often queue outside before it opens.
listeningExercises.prompt: What suggests the café is especially popular?
choices: It opens earlier than its competitors.
People line up before opening time.
listeningExercises.feedback: The result clause says customers often wait outside before opening.

listeningExercises.audioText: There is no such service at this hotel, so you need to arrange your own transport.
choices: Ask the hotel to send its shuttle.
Wait for the included transport service.
listeningExercises.feedback: No such service indicates the requested service is unavailable, so guests must arrange transport.

listeningExercises.audioText: The speakers were so loud that nobody could hear the safety announcement.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word expression immediately after “were”.
acceptedAnswers: so loud
listeningExercises.feedback: So modifies the adjective loud, which explains the consequence.

listeningExercises.audioText: We had such a great time at the festival that we stayed until midnight.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word expression immediately after “had”.
acceptedAnswers: such a great time
listeningExercises.feedback: Such a great time is a noun phrase describing a very enjoyable experience.
